fetched_contents.text: Performance comparison of RGB and multispectral vegetation indices based on machine learning for estimating Hopea hainanensis SPAD values under different shade conditions Abstract Reasonable cultivation is an important part of the protection work of endangered species. The timely and nondestructive monitoring of chlorophyll can provide a basis for the accurate management and intelligent development of cultivation. The image analysis method has been applied in the nutrient estimation of many economic crops, but information on endangered tree species is seldom reported. Moreover, shade control, as the common seedling management measure, has a significant impact on chlorophyll, but shade levels are rarely discussed in chlorophyll estimation and are used as variables to improve model accuracy. In this study, 2-year-old seedlings of tropical and endangered Hopea hainanensis were taken as the research object, and the SPAD value was used to represent the relative chlorophyll content. Based on the performance comparison of RGB and multispectral (MS) images using different algorithms, a low-cost SPAD estimation method combined with a machine learning algorithm that is adaptable to different shade conditions was proposed. The SPAD values changed significantly at different shade levels (p < 0.01), and 50% shade in the orthographic direction was conducive to chlorophyll accumulation in seedling leaves. The coefficient of determination (R2), root mean square error (RMSE), and average absolute percent error (MAPE) were used as indicators, and the models with dummy variables or random effects of shade greatly improved the goodness of fit, allowing better adaption to monitoring under different shade conditions. Most of the RGB and MS vegetation indices (VIs) were significantly correlated with the SPAD values, but some VIs exhibited multicollinearity (variance inflation factor (VIF) > 10). Among RGB VIs, RGRI had the strongest correlation, but multiple VIs filtered by the Lasso algorithm had a stronger ability to interpret the SPAD data, and there was no multicollinearity (VIF < 10). A comparison of the use of multiple VIs to estimate SPAD indicated that Random forest (RF) had the highest fitting ability, followed by Support vector regression (SVR), linear mixed effect model (LMM), and ordinary least squares regression (OLR). In addition, the performance of MS VIs was superior to that of RGB VIs. The R2 of the optimal model reached 0.9389 for the modeling samples and 0.8013 for the test samples. These findings reinforce the effectiveness of using VIs to estimate the SPAD value of H. hainanensis under different shade conditions based on machine learning and provide a reference for the selection of image data sources. However, the practical problems existing in protection and cultivation still pose huge challenges to the extensive cultivation of endangered plants. For instance, we have insufficient knowledge of the changes in physiological characteristics in the process of plant growth and cultivation, and we cannot obtain quantitative analysis results through a large number of destructive chemical experiments, so it is difficult to create a more suitable growth environment for endangered plants. Hopea hainanensis Merr. et Chun is a tropical endangered tree species mainly distributed in Hainan, China, and Nghe An, Vietnam (Song et al., 2020). Due to the slow growth rate and the sharp reduction in the number of these trees caused by human interference and destruction to the living environment, H. hainanensis has been rated as “endangered” (EN) by IUCN. Wild H. hainanensis is often grown in tropical rainforests and is shade tolerant, but corresponding investigations and research are still lacking. Chlorophyll is a compound that directly affects photosynthesis and is also an important indicator of plant growth. Some studies determined the most suitable light conditions for plant growth by analyzing changes in the chlorophyll content under different shade conditions (Senevirathna et al., 2003; Dai et al., 2009). Rapid and timely growth monitoring can be realized through rapid and nondestructive estimation of chlorophyll, thereby leading to more extensive artificial cultivation of endangered tree species, such as H. hainanensis. A portable chlorophyll analyzer can be used for the nondestructive determination of the chlorophyll content. The SPAD values measured by such an instrument have been shown to be effective in reflecting the chlorophyll content. Azaruddin et al. (2006) suggested that SPAD meter was potentially useful as an alternative to assess leaf chlorophyll of Hopea odorata. However, in practical applications, it is difficult to meet the data needs of large samples because of the manual nature of these measurements. Thanks to the development of automation, artificial intelligence and Internet of Things, the acquisition and transmission of image data is much easier than manual measurement. Image-based estimation method can be used as the basis of remote monitoring, even real-time monitoring. Reflection changes in nutrients and water in plants assessed by spectral information make the image-based estimation method feasible. Hyperspectral imaging technology can capture the rich spectral information of plants. In previous studies, the chlorophyll content was retrieved with high accuracy by selecting spectral indices highly correlated with the chlorophyll content from hyperspectral data to build models (Wang et al., 2019). Submission received: 6 January 2021 / Revised: 7 February 2021 / Accepted: 10 February 2021 / Published: 13 February 2021 Abstract Chlorophyll content in plant leaves is an essential indicator of the growth condition and the fertilization management effect of naked barley crops. The soil plant analysis development (SPAD) values strongly correlate with leaf chlorophyll contents. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV) can provide an efficient way to retrieve SPAD values on a relatively large scale with a high temporal resolution. But the UAV mounted with high-cost multispectral or hyperspectral sensors may be a tremendous economic burden for smallholder farmers. To overcome this shortcoming, we investigated the potential of UAV mounted with a commercial digital camera for estimating the SPAD values of naked barley leaves. We related 21 color-based vegetation indices (VIs) calculated from UAV images acquired from two flight heights (6.0 m and 50.0 m above ground level) in four different growth stages with SPAD values. Our results indicated that vegetation extraction and naked barley ears mask could improve the correlation between image-calculated vegetation indices and SPAD values. The VIs of ‘L*,’ ‘b*,’ ‘G − B’ and ‘2G − R − B’ showed significant correlations with SPAD values of naked barley leaves at both flight heights. The validation of the regression model showed that the index of ‘G-B’ could be regarded as the most robust vegetation index for predicting the SPAD values of naked barley leaves for different images and different flight heights. Our study demonstrated that the UAV mounted with a commercial camera has great potentiality in retrieving SPAD values of naked barley leaves under unstable photography conditions. It is significant for farmers to take advantage of the cheap measurement system to monitor crops. Graphical Abstract 1. Introduction Barley is the fourth largest cereal crop after maize, wheat and rice globally, with 7 percent of global cereal production. Barley production around the world is 159.0 million tons in 2019 [1]. It is a major food source for the people in the cool and semi-arid areas of the world, where wheat and other cereals are less adapted [2]. Due to the relatively harsh growing conditions, some suitable managements, especially nitrogen fertilizer, are necessary to sustain healthy growth and maximum yield production [3]. Moreover, leaf chlorophyll content has been proved to be related to nitrogen content in the crops and can be used as a fertilizer indicator during crop management [4,5,6,7,8]. The traditional chemical analysis of chlorophyll content has limitations of labor intensity, destruction and small measurement area. The soil and plant analysis development (SPAD) values measured by SPAD-502Plus Chlorophyll Meter (KONICA MINOLTA, Japan) can provide an accurate assessment of chlorophyll content in plant leaf in a non-destructive way [9,10,11,12,13]. But the measurement area of SPAD-502 is still limited and the meter can only be conducted on leaves one by one [14]. The method that could estimate SPAD values of leaves on a large scale and short time would help crop fertilizer management in the field. Nowadays, due to the development in color image acquirement, the color-based vegetation indices (VIs) from digital color cameras have been widely used in diagnosing crop physiological characteristics, including texture and shape features, leaf nitrogen and chlorophyll content [14,15,16,17]. For example, the vegetation indices based on red, green and blue (RGB) color system, such as ‘G/R,’ ‘R − B,’ ‘2G − R − B’ and ‘(R − B)/(R + B)’ are usually called “about-greenness” indices for analyzing plant characteristics, for estimating leaf chlorophyll and nitrogen contents or for distinguishing plant from the non-plant background [18,19,20,21,22]. In addition to the RGB-based vegetation indices, the vegetation indices based on other color systems, like International Commission on Illumination (CIE) L*a*b* color system and hue-saturation-intensity color system, also have been used in estimating vegetation status, like diagnosing macronutrient contents (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and magnesium) in crop leaves [23,24]. For a digital color camera, the image appearance (such as brightness and color temperature) would be influenced easily by illumination. The stable light condition could generally provide optimal light intensity and stability for the digital image capture and then the digital image would be convenient for the data analysis. On the contrary, the sunlight intensity changes would lead to different image appearances in different images [25]. In recent years, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV) have received more attention for their capability of covering a relatively large area in a short time and unlimited capture time, which could minimize the measurement error caused by changes in environmental factors [26,27,28,29,30]. Practical estimation of SPAD and grain yield from RGB data is grounded in the idea that color-based indices can approximate physiological or canopy-level traits without requiring expensive multispectral sensors. The evidence here indicates that RGB indices are used to estimate chlorophyll-related traits like SPAD and also to predict yield-like outcomes such as dry matter forage yield or biomass [N2-R4][N2-R5][N2-R2][N4-R5]. For SPAD specifically, the evidence shows that RGB-based vegetation indices are correlated with SPAD values, and some studies explicitly use them to estimate SPAD from UAV-based images, often combining feature selection and machine learning to improve accuracy under different shade conditions [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R5].

### How SPAD is estimated from RGB indices
SPAD estimation from RGB data is typically treated as a regression problem, where the RGB image-derived indices are used to predict the SPAD meter reading. The evidence suggests that indices like RGRI and others are strongly correlated with SPAD values, and that machine learning algorithms such as Random Forest or Support Vector Regression can be used to model the relationship [N1-F1]. The key assumptions are:
- The RGB indices are proxies for leaf chlorophyll content or leaf coloration related to chlorophyll [N2-F2][N3-R5].
- The image is acquired under conditions that are as close as possible to the SPAD measurement conditions, or the model explicitly incorporates variables such as shade level to account for lighting differences [N1-F1].
- The calibration relationship is not universal; it must be established locally or with a representative dataset because illumination, sensor settings, and canopy structure affect color appearance [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-R3].

### How grain yield is estimated and whether it depends on canopy-level or plot-level data
The evidence points to RGB indices being used to estimate yield-related outcomes such as dry matter forage yield and biomass, but it does not provide a single formula for grain yield in the same way it does for SPAD [N2-R4][N2-R5]. A study explicitly evaluated RGB-based vegetation indices to estimate dry matter forage yield on a recently established grassland, suggesting that yield estimation can be canopy-level or plot-level depending on the study design [N2-R4]. Another study used RGB indices to estimate cover crop biomass and nitrogen, showing that the indices can be used to infer canopy development and tissue nitrogen, which are traits that strongly influence yield potential [N7-R1][N7-R3].

The practical implication is that RGB-based yield estimation is often indirect: it depends on canopy-level canopy indices, plant height, coverage, or other ancillary metrics combined with the vegetation index [N7-R2]. The evidence also implies that plot-level validation is important, because the study on dry matter forage yield was evaluated on a recently established grassland, and yield is inherently plot- or field-scale rather than individual-plant-scale [N2-R4].

### Common challenges in translating RGB estimates to real trait values
The evidence identifies several practical limitations. First, RGB indices are sensitive to illumination changes and unstable photography conditions, which can reduce the correlation with SPAD or other traits [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-R3]. Second, RGB indices may not account for canopy structure or background effects well, especially under degraded or heterogeneous conditions [N4-R3]. Third, the evidence repeatedly notes that RGB indices can have high correlation with traits, but not always sufficient performance on their own; multispectral methods often outperform RGB in practice, and machine learning is often used to improve robustness [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R5].

Other challenges include:
- **Sensor calibration**: The evidence implies that RGB values must be calibrated or normalized because the same color can appear different under different lighting or sensor conditions [N2-F2][N5-F3].
- **Multicollinearity**: In SPAD estimation, some RGB indices exhibit multicollinearity, which can reduce model interpretability and performance [N1-F1].
- **Generalization across species and growth stages**: The study on naked barley leaves explicitly tested indices across different flight heights and growth stages, showing that robustness can vary with context [N2-F2].
- **Limited physical basis**: RGB indices are often empirical or semi-empirical, so they may not directly measure the target trait; instead, they are proxies that must be validated against ground-truth measurements [N2-F2][N4-R2].

Overall, RGB-based estimation of SPAD and yield is practical but requires careful calibration, context-specific validation, and often auxiliary measurements to improve accuracy [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R4][N4-R2].

The mathematical formulation of RGB-based vegetation indices is typically derived from basic color-space operations, and the evidence here shows that they are often simple ratios, differences, or combinations of red (R), green (G), and blue (B) pixel values. The sources also emphasize the importance of normalization, wavelength-specific coefficients, and calibration, because RGB values are not direct reflectance values and can be influenced by sensor settings, lighting, and image processing [N2-F2][N5-F3][N6-F2].

### How each index is computed from RGB reflectance values
The evidence indicates that RGB indices are usually computed using the R, G, and B channels of a digital image. A review source notes that RGB-based vegetation indices are calculated from UAV images, and it gives examples such as ‘G/R,’ ‘R − B,’ ‘2G − R − B,’ and ‘(R − B)/(R + B)’ [N2-F2]. Another source lists RGB color-space indices and describes some basic operations, including intensity, saturation, and other derived values [N5-F3]. These formulas are not strictly reflectance-based in the multispectral sense, but they are commonly treated as proxies for narrow-band reflectance proxies or as empirical vegetation indices in RGB imagery.

### Whether it uses simple ratios, differences, or more complex combinations
The evidence shows a mix of simple and more complex combinations:
- **Simple ratios**: Formulas such as G/R and (R − B)/(R + B) are explicitly identified as common RGB indices [N2-F2][N5-F3].
- **Differences**: R − B and 2G − R − B are also described as examples of RGB-based indices [N2-F2].
- **More complex combinations**: Some studies combine vegetation indices with image texture, and one source notes that RGB indices are often used in combination with other image features such as texture and shape [N2-R3]. The evidence also suggests that machine learning models may be used to combine multiple indices, improving performance beyond any single index [N1-F1].

### The role of normalization, wavelength-specific coefficients, and calibration
Normalization is an important step in making RGB indices comparable across images or sensors. The evidence implies that RGB values must be calibrated or normalized because the same physical condition can produce different RGB values under different lighting or sensor conditions [N2-F2][N5-F3]. It also notes that RGB-based indices can be used to estimate narrow-band reflectance indices or photosynthetic parameters, which suggests that they are often treated as proxies for more physically meaningful reflectance bands rather than true multispectral measurements [N5-R4].

Calibration is explicitly required. The evidence states that UAV-mounted cameras can provide useful SPAD estimates under unstable photography conditions, but the study emphasizes that vegetation extraction and masking improved the correlation between image-derived vegetation indices and SPAD values [N2-F2]. This implies that preprocessing steps such as background subtraction, object masking, and normalization are necessary to improve the reliability of the indices [N2-F2].

Wavelength-specific coefficients are not directly provided in the evidence, but the implication is strong: RGB indices are inherently limited by the three narrow color bands available in standard cameras, whereas true reflectance indices rely on spectrally separated bands [N5-R4]. The evidence also notes that RGB indices can be used to estimate narrow-band indices and photosynthetic parameters, which indicates that the RGB values are often treated as proxies for spectrally resolved reflectance rather than true multispectral measurements [N5-R4].

### Overall implications for derivation
Taken together, the evidence suggests that RGB indices are mathematically simple in form but require careful calibration and normalization because their derivation is empirical rather than physically derived from calibrated reflectance. The most common formulas are simple ratios, differences, or combinations of R, G, and B values, and the best performance is often achieved when those indices are combined with additional image features or machine learning models [N2-F2][N5-F3][N2-R3][N1-F1]. Calibration and normalization are therefore essential for translating RGB values into reliable vegetation indices [N2-F2][N5-F3].

RGB-to-reflectance conversion is a critical step in improving the reliability of vegetation indices, because raw RGB values are not direct reflectance values and are highly sensitive to sensor settings, lighting, and image-processing artifacts. The evidence here supports that conversion or proxy-based approaches are needed to make RGB values usable for more physically meaningful vegetation indices [N5-R3][N5-R4][N6-R1][N6-R2].

### How RGB values are converted to reflectance or narrow-band proxies
The evidence shows that RGB values are often converted to reflectance-like proxies or used as narrow-band proxies rather than true multispectral reflectance. A research discussion explicitly asks about converting spectral bands to reflectance, which is a common problem when working with RGB images [N6-R1]. The same source also notes that RGB indices can be used to estimate narrow-band reflectance indices and photosynthetic parameters, indicating that RGB values are treated as proxies for spectrally resolved reflectance [N5-R4]. In addition, the pliman source describes conversion from RGB to Lab and other derived values, showing that RGB can be transformed into other color-space values that may be used as proxies for vegetation properties [N6-R2].

The evidence does not provide a single universal RGB-to-reflectance formula, but it does suggest that such conversion is typically needed because RGB values are not calibrated reflectance values. The practical implication is that RGB images alone are insufficient for accurate vegetation index derivation; they must be converted into reflectance-like quantities or used as narrow-band proxies [N5-R3][N5-R4].

### What calibration or sensor-specific steps are required
The evidence emphasizes several calibration and sensor-specific steps:
- **Sensor-specific preprocessing**: The UAV study notes that vegetation extraction and naked barley ears masking improved the correlation between image-derived vegetation indices and SPAD values [N2-F2]. This implies that preprocessing such as segmentation, masking, and normalization is essential.
- **Normalization**: The RGB-based SPAD study states that RGB indices are correlated with SPAD values, but the model performance depends on local calibration and shade conditions, indicating that normalization or scaling is necessary [N1-F1].
- **Illumination conditions**: The evidence repeatedly notes that RGB-based vegetation indices are sensitive to unstable photography conditions and illumination changes, so calibration must account for lighting variability [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-R3].
- **Color-space transformation**: The pliman source shows that RGB can be converted to Lab, which may help in separating color components and improving index stability [N6-R2].

### How this affects the reliability of vegetation indices
The evidence clearly indicates that failure to convert RGB values properly can reduce index reliability. First, RGB indices are inherently limited by the three narrow color channels of a camera, so they are less informative than multispectral reflectance data [N5-R4]. Second, without proper calibration, the same biological condition can appear different in RGB values, leading to inconsistent index values [N2-F2]. Third, the evidence shows that RGB indices can correlate well with traits such as SPAD, but their performance may degrade under heterogeneous conditions or when multispectral methods are used as a benchmark [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R5].

The reliability implications are therefore substantial:
- **Robustness to lighting and sensor changes**: Proper calibration and normalization are needed to make the indices stable across images and flight conditions [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-R3].
- **Sensitivity to preprocessing**: Masking, segmentation, and normalization improve the correlation between indices and target traits, showing that reliability depends on careful image processing [N2-F2].
- **Empirical limitation**: RGB indices are empirical proxies, so their reliability depends on the calibration dataset and the trait being estimated [N2-F2][N5-R4].

Overall, RGB-to-reflectance conversion or proxy construction is necessary for reliable vegetation indices, but it requires sensor-specific calibration, normalization, and careful preprocessing to mitigate the limitations of RGB color space [N5-R3][N5-R4][N6-R1][N6-R2].

The aggregate evidence indicates that RGB-based vegetation indices are most frequently used for plant traits related to chlorophyll content, nitrogen, biomass, canopy development, and yield-like outcomes, rather than a single universal trait. The sources consistently mention SPAD, biomass, nitrogen, canopy coverage, leaf nitrogen concentration, and dry matter forage yield as the target traits [N1-R4][N2-R4][N2-R5][N7-R1][N7-R3][N7-R2]. The most frequently named RGB indices in the evidence are simple color-ratio and difference indices such as G/R, R − B, 2G − R − B, and (R − B)/(R + B), with additional mention of RGRI and related combinations [N2-F2][N5-F3][N1-F1].

### Which RGB indices are most frequently used for plant traits
The most frequently mentioned RGB indices are:
- **G/R** [N2-F2]
- **R − B** [N2-F2]
- **2G − R − B** [N2-F2]
- **(R − B)/(R + B)** [N2-F2]
- **RGRI** [N1-F1]

These indices appear repeatedly in the evidence as examples of RGB vegetation indices used for plant trait estimation. The pliman source also lists RGB color-space indices and derived values such as intensity and saturation, which are broader color-based metrics rather than the narrow vegetation-index subset [N5-F3].

### What plant traits each index is associated with
The evidence associates RGB indices with several plant traits:
- **Chlorophyll/SPAD-related traits**: The study on SPAD estimation explicitly uses RGB indices to predict SPAD values, and the review notes that RGB indices are useful for estimating leaf chlorophyll content and nitrogen content [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R5].
- **Biomass-related traits**: RGB indices are used to estimate canopy development, tissue nitrogen, and biomass in cover crops, including medium red clover and other forage legumes [N7-R1][N7-R3].
- **Canopy and coverage traits**: RGB indices are used in conjunction with canopy coverage and plant height to estimate leaf nitrogen concentration and biomass in summer maize [N7-R2].
- **Yield-like traits**: RGB indices are used to estimate dry matter forage yield and other yield-related outcomes [N2-R4][N2-R5].
- **Nitrogen-related traits**: RGB indices are associated with tissue nitrogen and nitrogen content in cover crops and maize [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3].

### Whether the index is designed for SPAD, biomass, yield, or other traits
The evidence shows that the indices are not narrowly tied to one trait, but rather are used across multiple trait domains:
- **SPAD**: RGB indices are specifically used for SPAD estimation, often combined with machine learning and shade-level variables [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R5].
- **Biomass**: RGB indices are used to estimate biomass and canopy development [N7-R1][N7-R3].

These indices are typically simple ratios, differences, or combinations of the red (R), green (G), and blue (B) channels of RGB images [N9][N2-F2]. They are used to estimate a broad range of plant traits, including:

- **SPAD or chlorophyll-related traits**: RGB indices are directly used to predict SPAD values, and the evidence shows that they are correlated with leaf chlorophyll content and nitrogen content [N8][N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R5].

- **Canopy and coverage traits**: RGB indices are combined with canopy coverage and plant height to estimate leaf nitrogen concentration and biomass [N7-R2].
- **Yield-like outcomes**: RGB indices are used to estimate dry matter forage yield and other yield-related outcomes [N2-R4][N2-R5].

In other words, the same index family is reused across multiple trait domains, which means the indices are not trait-specific in a rigid sense; they are broad proxies that must be validated for each target trait [N8][N10].

### 2) How they are mathematically formulated

The mathematical formulation of RGB-based indices is typically derived from basic color-space operations. The evidence shows that they are often:

- **simple ratios**, such as G/R and (R − B)/(R + B),
- **differences**, such as R − B,
- **more complex combinations**, such as 2G − R − B,
- and sometimes combined with other image features, such as texture or shape, before being used in prediction models [N9][N2-F2][N2-R3].

A key point from the branch reports is that **RGB values are not direct reflectance values**, so they must be treated as proxies or narrow-band proxies rather than true multispectral reflectance [N5-R4][N9]. This distinction is important because it explains why the indices are empirical and why they often depend on calibration.

### 3) Role of normalization, wavelength-specific coefficients, and calibration

The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that normalization and calibration are essential for making RGB indices reliable. The branch reports indicate that:

- RGB values are sensitive to illumination, sensor settings, and image-processing artifacts, so **normalization** is needed to make the indices comparable across images and conditions [N9][N11].

In other words, the RGB index is a proxy for spectrally resolved reflectance rather than a true multispectral measurement [N5-R4][N9].

SPAD estimation from RGB data is usually treated as a regression problem: RGB-derived indices are used to predict the SPAD meter reading. - the indices are calibrated to the target trait,
- the sensor and lighting conditions are as close as possible to the ground-truth measurements,
- the indices are validated on a representative dataset,
- and the system accounts for canopy structure, background effects, and illumination changes [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R2][N11].
